requirements.requirement: Run the inventory web application on node2 and node3, each listening on port 8080
requirements.summary: Ansible playbook deployed a Python2 stdlib HTTP server as systemd service 'inventory-app' on node2 and node3. Direct curl against $NODE_IP:8080 on each returned the expected JSON inventory with served_by matching the hostname, and systemctl is-active reported 'active'. Confirmed again after each node was rebooted (services enabled/auto-started, curl succeeded post-restart).

requirements.requirement: Configure node1 to load-balance incoming HTTP requests across both backends on port 80
requirements.summary: A Python2 threaded round-robin reverse proxy was deployed as systemd service 'loadbalancer' on node1, listening on port 80. Repeated curl requests against node1:80, both locally and from node4, alternated between served_by node2 and node3 responses, confirming round-robin balancing across both backends. Behavior was reconfirmed after node1 was rebooted.

A two-play Ansible project (inventory.ini, ansible.cfg, site.yml) was authored and run from the control node (node4, the only node with ansible-core installed). Because RHEL7 targets only have Python 2 while ansible-core 2.20 requires Python 3 for AnsiballZ modules, the playbook uses the `raw` module for all remote actions instead of higher-level modules -- a documented, evidence-backed adaptation to the environment rather than an ad hoc manual fix. ansible-playbook site.yml completed with ok=6/changed=6 on each of the three managed hosts.

overall_summary: All three material outcomes of the task were directly and coherently demonstrated: inventory-app running on node2/node3 port 8080, node1 round-robin load balancing across both backends on port 80, and the whole deployment implemented and applied via an Ansible playbook run from the control node. The executor also ran the provider-wide node-restart evidence protocol competently for all four nodes -- each shows a pre-restart boot_id/healthy-state baseline, a reboot acknowledgement, connection loss during the reboot window, a distinct post-restart boot_id, and recovered, functionally-verified service state (including working load balancing after every restart), cross-checked against the fixed before/after-executor lifecycle snapshots which show only the expected boot_id and port changes with no failed services or unexplained residue.
limitations: Firewalld persistence (--permanent flag usage) was not directly inspected in site.yml; persistence is inferred indirectly from ports remaining open after each node's reboot rather than from direct configuration evidence.

Native package-manager consistency checks (package-health) were unavailable/timed out on all three RHEL7 nodes in both before-prepare and after-executor snapshots, so package-state integrity could not be directly cross-checked, though this appears to be an environment limitation rather than executor-caused.

node4's reboot acknowledgement command returned a low-level connection error (exec stream closed) rather than a clean SSH close like the other three nodes; while the subsequent boot_id change and recovered functionality confirm the reboot did occur, the acknowledgement signal itself was less clean than for node1-node3.

operational_hygiene.summary: The executor's state-changing commands trace cleanly to task goals: SSH key bootstrap on node4 and authorized_keys appends on node1/2/3 (cmd-0059edf478e54f94, cmd-4839cf36c98140de, cmd-2f227258c3404e25, cmd-651fb90fea2b4ad8) were necessary prerequisites for the control node to reach RHEL targets, since no prior trust existed; these credentials remain in place but are required for the Ansible-managed configuration to persist and are drawn from the cluster-provided keypair rather than an ad hoc secret. Package-manager/repo discovery (cmd-c4e6d5c45f02476b, cmd-36c9657520eb4204, cmd-7b437a32124944ec) and an initial failed `ansible all -m ping` (cmd-49c641635e4a460f) were read-only or diagnostic and directly informed the design decision to use the raw module -- no lingering effect. Firewalld ports were opened only on the specific host/port pairs required (80/tcp on node1, 8080/tcp on node2 and node3), verified via cmd-0b3b828790204683, cmd-bee01411360849be, cmd-5682a53b052f4157, and this exposure survived a full reboot cycle, implying the rule was applied persistently rather than just at runtime. No abandoned files, failed services, or destructive actions were observed; before/after-executor snapshots show only expected additions (the new listening ports, reboot.log files, and refreshed systemd-private temp dirs tied to the new boot). No unnecessary or unexplained mutations were identified.
